scores.reason: Consumer, self-directed, liquid-money field experiment showing a default-related nudge moves the headline metric without moving the outcome that matters at six months — exactly the vanity-enrolment trade-off the brief's entry decision turns on (C2, C4).

EU multi-country experiment quantifying both default effect sizes and the reputational cost (lower advisor-honesty ratings, especially when defaults are refused) — directly informs the dark-pattern risk and level framing (C4, C5, C3).

The classic anchoring-at-the-default-rate evidence (C1, C2, C3), but it is an old employer-plan study with broken metadata (no year, RePEc listing) selected on score in a brief that explicitly says recent work matters more; relevant by analogy, not central.

Recent, rigorous evidence that auto-enrolment's steady-state savings effect is far smaller than headline enrolment suggests once attrition and withdrawal are counted — the strongest available support/contradiction test for the brief's central premise (C1, C2).
AER 2025 study measuring exactly the persistence question the brief asks (gains at 12 months attenuate by 36) plus distributional effects; directly changes the entry decision (C1, C2, C5).

Useful recent review covering short- vs long-term default effects and engagement costs, satisfying the brief's request for a synthesis, but employer-plan focused and narrative rather than effect-size-bearing; its own why_it_matters concedes it is background.

Large-scale recent estimate (23pp) with the moderators the brief needs — default effect weakens when opt-out is easy and incentives low, and heterogeneity by enrollee knowledge speaks to who is captured passively (C1, C5).

Restates the passivity/disengagement concern already established with real evidence by ranks 4-6, contributes no original data or effect sizes, appears in a low-credibility venue, and its mitigation suggestions are generic; shares the topic without adding decision-relevant information.

Foundational slot: the origin paper for the active-choice design the brief names as one of its three entry options, with a transferable enhanced-active-choice technique; a newcomer weighing C6 must know it.

Foundational slot: the canonical active-vs-passive-saver result (85% passive, unmoved by incentives) that the newer persistence and heterogeneity papers in this list are arguing with; essential background for the opt-in/opt-out/active-choice framing.
